groundTruthNarrative: At 10:38 UTC on 3 March the edge protection vendor, Corvane, automatically applied rule pack 2026.03.1 to Oxleigh's mobile API. A new rule, AUTO-LIB-17, blocks requests to the password-login path when the user-agent is the default 'nettle-http' library string and no edge session cookie is present. Oxleigh's Android app sends every API call through nettle-http with that default user-agent. The iOS app uses a custom user-agent, and quick-unlock uses a different path. From 10:41, about 9,700 Android password submissions a day got a vendor 403 and never reached the auth service. Android login success fell from 97.1% to about 88.4%. Android 6.14 happened to start a staged rollout at 09:00 the same day, with a redesigned password screen, so leadership blamed the release. But 6.14 made up only 5% of attempts, and every older version failed the same way at the same minute. Devices with and without the March OS patch also failed at identical rates. The blocked traffic came from established customer installs, not credential stuffing. The auth service's token change affected both platforms and changed nothing. The vendor's tenant-wide figures hid a problem confined to one path. Whether the redesign raises typing errors cannot be determined, because few password submissions have reached a credential check since 10:41. The fix is to set the new rules to log-only on that path and confirm recovery.

answers.rationale: C1 shows versions 6.11, 6.12 and 6.13 dropped to the same ~88.4% as 6.14. All versions began failing in the same minute (10:41 on 3 March), and 6.14 was only 5% of attempts. A 5% share cannot produce an 8.7-point drop. The timing and the password-screen redesign in E1/E2 are coincidental.

C2 shows a new rule, activated at 10:38, blocking requests that carry the nettle-http user-agent on the password path from 10:41. That is about 9,700 blocks a day, from established Android installs. E2 says the Android app uses nettle-http for every call. C1 shows the added failures are all server-rejected 403s on password submissions from 10:41, while quick-unlock (not covered by the rule) is unchanged. C6's tenant-wide reassurance is outweighed by these path-level counts.

E5: the KPI counts only attempts from installed apps, not scripted traffic. C2: the blocked requests came from 41,300 app installs, 92% of which had logged in successfully before, averaging 1.6 blocked requests each over the week. That is a customer pattern, not a credential-stuffing pattern. E4's claim is an inference from the 28 Feb web event.
C1: success is 88.2–88.6% on every Android OS version and 88.4% on devices both with and without the March security patch. The failures do not track the OS update.

C1: 6.14 had only 38 password attempts before the blocking began. Since then few password submissions reach a credential check, so credential-error rates for the redesign cannot be measured. The claim is still possible but unestablished.

E3: the token-lifetime change applied equally to iOS and Android and affects only session expiry, yet E1 shows iOS flat. C2 adds that the auth service's 401/5xx rates on forwarded Android requests did not change.

Timing: the rule was activated at 10:38 and the first block came at 10:41, the same minute the client 403s began (C1). Mechanism: the rule matches nettle-http on the password path, which only the Android app sends (C2, E2). Covariation: about 9,700 blocks a day against about 9,400 added failures. Main rivals ruled out: all app and OS versions are affected equally (C1), and iOS, web and quick-unlock have zero hits.
C1 counts directly against the link. Versions that never received 6.14 fell by the same amount at the same minute, and 6.14 carried only 5% of attempts.

The rise in calls coincides with the login drop. But annual fee notices went out on 2 March, reason codes are unreliable, and 57% of calls were default-coded (E6). C8 confirms the rise cannot be split between causes. The two co-occur, but causation of the 18% rise is not established.
The metric excludes scripted traffic (E5). The requests that make up the drop came from established customer installs at low per-device volume (C2). Evidence counts against the link itself.

This targets the established mechanism and is reversible. Log-only keeps visibility, and the step includes checking that success recovers. It restores the pre-3 March posture on one path only. That posture, with rate limits and lockout, contained the 28 Feb attack (E4, C7). The new rule is blocking customers, not attackers (C2).
C2 shows the edge is already blocking legitimate customers. Raising sensitivity would block more of them, and no live rival is helped by it. The credential-stuffing explanation is contradicted.

The edge-blocked attempts are real customers using installed apps (E5, C2). Excluding them would hide the failure from executives under any hypothesis. C11 already shows how dashboards that count blocks as 'protected' made the problem invisible.

6.14 is not implicated (C1), and crash data is normal (C4). Continuing the rollout while tracking login outcomes by version is reasonable. It does nothing to fix the customer impact, so it is not among the best actions.

This would help if the redesign raises credential errors (H5). That is currently unmeasurable (C1). A future release could reverse the change, so it does no lasting damage, but committing to it now is not justified.
The top action, A1, is substantive. Timing, mechanism, covariation and rival exclusion (C1 + C2) justify committing to it, and it is scoped, reversible and self-verifying.

authoringNotes: Trap structure: Android 6.14 started rolling out at 09:00 on 3 March and redesigned the password screen, which is exactly where the failures sit (E1, E2). The edge rule-pack update is one 'standard, pre-approved' line among five changes, with no time given (E3). Security Operations pushes a bot explanation (E4), and the vendor says nothing changed for legitimate traffic (C6). C1 is the only item with failure rates by app version, rollout share and OS patch status. It alone settles H1, R2 and H4. C2 has no version data, and the X-Client header and user-agent carry no app version. C3 shows 6.14 upgraded nettle-http, so with C2 alone a reader cannot rule out that 6.14 introduced the matching user-agent. C2 is the only item giving the rule-activation time, the rule logic, block counts and the device-history pattern. It alone settles R1 (causal), H2, H3/R4 and the A1/SUFF commitment. C1 alone shows a server-side 403 onset at 10:41 but cannot tie it to the vendor change, whose time is missing from E3. The rollout percentage appears only in C1; C13 was written so it does not leak it. C5 has no platform breakdown, so it cannot localise the loss. C10, C11 and C14 hint at the edge without settling anything. H6 is already contradicted from the initial file (it affects both platforms, and iOS is flat). R3 stays association-only under every item because of the fee-notice confound and unreliable coding. Numbers reconcile: pre-period overall success is (96,700×0.972 + 7,500×0.96)/104,200 = 97.1%. Post-period is (96,900×0.972 + 10,600×0.082)/107,500 = 88.4%. E1's 88.7% includes the partial 3 March. iOS figures in C12 also reconcile. All names (Oxleigh Mutual, Corvane, nettle-http, people) are fictional.
